paragraph:
The Village That Refused to Be Sold

By noon, the mayor had threatened to close the (fairground), a (tarantula) had escaped from the school’s animal tent, and Nora Bell had discovered that somebody intended to (entomb) her grandmother’s letters beneath a supermarket car park. Only the first two events had attracted public attention. Bellweather possessed an impressive (aptitude) for (hysteria), but its response to paperwork was usually (torpid). Nora, who had returned to sell her grandmother’s house, had expected a quiet weekend. Instead, she stood beside a (hydrangea), holding an (embossed) envelope and wondering whether to (buttonhole) the mayor before or after his speech.

The (addressee) was Eleanor Marsh, (née) Bell. Inside, a solicitor referred to the market hall as property held for the village “in (permanence)”. This was difficult to reconcile with the mayor’s proposal to (dismantle) it on Monday. Nora’s grandmother had spent forty years there, teaching children to (knead) bread and adults to (haggle) over heating bills. She had considered (servitude) to a committee an honour, provided one could occasionally (offend) its chairman. Nora had inherited her (rosewood) sewing box, a silver (bangle), and a letter instructing her not to let “that (shrewd) little man” sell the hall. She had assumed this was a final expression of an old (vendetta).

Mayor Pike was already onstage. An (unremarkable) man with a carefully trimmed (goatee), he became (formidable) when equipped with a microphone. His opening (preamble) concerned efficiency; the next ten minutes were (soporific) enough to (addle) a caffeinated horse. The hall, he explained, was a (relic), its plumbing (substandard), its restoration practically (undoable). Demolition would provide a (springboard) for prosperity. From a (cluttered) table nearby, the custodian watched with a (sardonic) expression. “He can (expound) till Christmas,” he told Nora. “Still doesn’t explain why he’s selling a building he doesn’t own.”

The custodian was called Kit. His (stubble), patched (tunic), and permanent (grimace) made him resemble an unemployed sorcerer. He was (irascible), frequently (irritable), and not especially (lovable), although he had once spent a night repairing the nursery’s heating for nothing. People dismissed him as an (eccentric). Pike preferred “(lunatic)”. Kit called Pike a (dunderhead), then apologised to an actual schoolboy who had overheard him. “I knew your grandmother (firsthand),” he said. “She wasn’t always right. But she could (deduce) a dishonest arrangement from the way a man folded his invoices.” He examined the letter. For the first time, his expression (clouded).

Usually, nothing could (perturb) Kit. A burst pipe earned a casual wave; a complaint earned an (unruffled) invitation to fix it yourself. But this letter could (topple) the entire redevelopment scheme. “You’d better (heed) this,” he said. Nora asked whether he knew a lawyer. “Several. Most won’t (oblige) me any more.” He searched his pockets and produced a (wad) of old receipts. Among them was a telephone number. It was the first (vestige) of a plan.

Around them, Bellweather pursued its (innumerable) small pleasures. Children could (frolic) beside a (collapsible) castle while adults queued for a (chipolata), a spoonful of (custard), or a jar of (marmalade). The gardening society displayed a (begonia), a (periwinkle), and some unusually vigorous (lovage). Beyond a (shrub), a youth orchestra attempted a (serenade), its (rhythmic) confidence considerably stronger than its tuning. A baker used a (ladle) to pour batter while her husband tried to (mince) onions and (shoo) a dog simultaneously. The smell of hot sugar was a welcome (tonic). Nora had intended to buy lunch, take a (siesta), and leave. Now she could barely (nibble) a biscuit.

From the stage, Pike’s promises continued. Kit regarded them as expensive (waffle). A shopkeeper beside him preferred “(bilge)”. Neither man would (applaud), though the mayor’s supporters responded with conspicuous (glee). A boy began to (mimic) Pike’s gestures until his mother stopped him. “He’s not a (hysteric),” she said, “and neither are you.” The boy adopted an expression of wounded dignity. Ordinarily, the scene would have amused Nora. Today, she could only (brood) over the envelope.

Kit led her through the hall’s side entrance. A (bramble) had claimed the drain, and (honeysuckle) pressed against the glass. Inside, the air smelled (stale), with a (tinge) of something (acrid). A (puddle) reflected a plaster (cherub) whose (resemblance) to the mayor was unfortunate. Paint had begun to (flake); one wall was (riddled) with holes. A cupboard contained (rancid) polish, a (blob) of hardened glue, and a single petrified (crumb). “There’s neglect,” Nora said. “Certainly,” Kit replied. “But being a (slob) isn’t the same as owning the place.” From behind a panel came a soft (throb), as though the building had a nervous heart.

Kit stopped. The noise stopped too. The upper floor was supposed to be (uninhabited). Nora felt a (prickle) beneath her collar. Kit picked up a (spade), then reconsidered and put it down. “No (bloodshed),” he said. “Bad for the insurance.” They began to (ascend). On the landing, Nora had to (disentangle) her sleeve from a nail that continued to (protrude) through the rail. A door stood open. Beyond it, an (unaccompanied) boy wearing a (balaclava) was trying to (manhandle) an old trunk onto a wheeled (bogie). He looked (cornered). Then his foot slipped, and the trunk landed with a (thud).

The boy was Milo, Pike’s nephew, a (timid) sixteen-year-old with a (freckle) on his nose and a spectacular (pimple) on his chin. He removed the mask, revealing a (pallid), thoroughly (anguished) face. “Dust,” he explained, waving at the fabric. “I couldn’t find anything else.” He had expected to move rubbish, not meet witnesses. Kit began to (goad) him, but Nora intervened. She would not have a frightened child (frogmarched) out of the room before anyone had heard his account. She asked Milo to sit down. An (unprovoked) attack would merely (enrage) his uncle and (discourage) the one person who might (divulge) what was happening.

“I was told to clear it (beforehand),” Milo said. “Before Monday. That (bloke) from the buyers said nobody would mind.” Nora asked him not to (fib). He stared at his shoes. “I’m not.” Kit found a (penknife) and (unscrewed) a loose brass plate on the trunk. Its lid would not (budge), so Nora gave the corner a careful (nudge). There was a metallic (crackle). An internal catch had jammed; a small (gib) in the fitting had slipped. Together they managed to (dislodge) it. “Don’t (mangle) the documents,” Kit warned. “They’re worth more than the box.” Milo tried to (exhale) without sounding frightened.

Inside lay a (jumble) of accounts, photographs, and theatrical costumes. A (puce) folder was tied with (braid). Beneath a moth-eaten (bedspread), Nora found a ledger recording payments in (specie), rent for an (orphanage) benefit, and the postal (poundage) charged on relief parcels. One invoice concerned a donated (bedstead), its matching (headboard), and transport by (barge). A photograph showed her grandmother standing (astride) a broken bicycle, laughing. Nora had come prepared to (renounce) her attachment to Bellweather. Instead, the sight made her (wince). She sat on the trunk, suddenly unable to perform the (businesslike) indifference she had practised all week.

The costumes belonged to an amateur production about a fraudulent emperor. There was a (toga), a battered (monocle), a rubber (tentacle), and an empty (scabbard). Two envelopes contained false facial hair: “(mustache)” on one, “(moustache)” on the other. Even the props committee had managed to (quibble). A sketch showed a mechanical monster, part (cockatrice), part (kelpie), intended to (disgorge) paper scraps. Its jaws had been carved with such care that someone had labelled a (ruga) on the palate. “Your grandmother did that,” Kit said. “Dental nurse before she retired.” A (scarab) brooch fell from the costume pile. Nora remembered it immediately. She had been allowed to wear it when she played a (pixie).

Memory began to (overtake) her. She recalled an (eerie) blue light, the audience’s (hubbub), and her own (frantic) effort not to (stumble). Her grandmother had whispered, “Whatever may (betide), keep going.” A wooden (cupid) had fallen from the scenery; a stage (grenade) had proved a (dud). The emperor had improvised an (antic) bow and turned disaster into comedy. Now, tucked into the ledger, lay a programme with a (legible) note: all proceeds would protect the hall from private sale. The promise was neither (vapid) nor vague. Nora felt the first (tingle) of anger. “Where’s the actual deed?”

The question broke Kit’s own (reverie). He remembered a midsummer (solstice) meeting, an argument about a proposed sale, and the documents being locked away afterwards. Years of (strife) had followed, then everyone involved had grown old. It seemed absurd that a promise could (elude) a village simply because nobody remembered its filing system. “Unless,” Kit said, “it’s still here, (perchance).” His hopeful formality almost made Nora smile. She began checking every pocket and sleeve, waiting for the missing paper to (resurface).

Milo began to (fumble) through the papers. “There was another box.” His voice fell to a (mumble). It had been taken to the waste container that morning. Kit uttered a (swearword) of considerable force. Nora was briefly too (unnerved) to move. Then her grandmother’s instructions seemed almost (prophetic). They must (retrace) the boy’s route, (rummage) through the container, and hope rain had not reduced the contents to pulp. Kit wanted to (allege) a deliberate attempt to destroy evidence. Nora insisted they establish the facts first. A (shred) of suspicion would not (suffice), however satisfying the anticipated (comeuppance).

Outside, the mayor’s speech had given way to a pet parade. A (wolfhound) with abundant (saliva) investigated a (boarhound), while a woman tried to (soothe) a baby beginning to (teethe). In the animal tent, an (iguana) rested beside a model (loggerhead) turtle. The escaped spider had been found in a box of (seaweed) behind the aquarium. Its owner complained about the (stigma) attached to harmless hobbies. A blue (budgie), restored to its (birdcage), supplied a piercing commentary. Nora attempted to (wend) through the crowd. Kit followed, having to (fend) off a determined organiser who wanted him to judge the (plumage) competition.

The waste container stood beyond the (churchyard), where an old (stile) opened onto the delivery yard. Nora’s shoe caught a (pebble), and she nearly suffered an (overbalance) as she climbed across. Milo offered a (supple) branch for support. On the ground, (woodlice) scattered beside a nest that Kit thought belonged to (dormice). A (vole) vanished before anyone could (trample) it. Above them, birds were almost ready to (fledge) on a stone (ledge). Everything seemed determined to carry on with its ordinary business. Nora envied that certainty. Her own plans had fallen by the (wayside) in less than an hour.

Someone had thrown kitchen waste over the box. The smell was (putrid). A discarded (artichoke), a strip of orange (rind), and an entire ruined (blancmange) lay across the papers. Kit tried to (dredge) them out with a stick. Milo had to (writhe) between two bags to reach the bottom, muttering that he might (puke). “Don’t,” said Kit. “We have enough material.” Nora held open a sack while a persistent (midge) made her (jiggle) her shoulder. At last a water-stained packet emerged. A (telltale) blue seal remained (discernible) beneath a (smudge). She felt almost (ecstatic), until a familiar voice said, “Put that down.”

Milo made a startled (lunge) away from the container. His elbow struck its rim, sending a sheet of paper sailing. Nora managed to catch it on the (verge) of the drain. Pike’s arrival had been almost too well timed, but this was a (fluke), not evidence of surveillance. Beyond the fence, a volunteer was complaining about a dog’s (turd); another was attempting to (dole) out rain covers. The contrast between their ordinary troubles and Nora’s sudden predicament was enough to (dumbfound) her.

Pike stood at the gate. He looked (livid). His (offhand) manner had vanished, replaced by the (palpable) fury of a man losing control of his afternoon. “This is (despicable),” he said. Kit started to answer, but Nora raised a hand before the argument could become a (scuffle). She would not let a quarrel about manners (override) the evidence. Pike accused them of (sabotage), described the expedition as a (rampage), and said they had no right to (meddle). The last word was a mistake. Nora had spent twenty years being told not to interfere. She discovered she no longer cared.

“Did you tell Milo to remove these?” she asked. Pike tried to (evade) the question with an account of insurance. Kit gave a (snide) laugh. Milo stared at the grass. “You can (chide) me later,” Nora said. “Answer him now.” Pike’s silence seemed to (derange) the boy more than anger would have. Finally Milo spoke. The mayor had asked for the rooms to be emptied, but the buyer’s representative had specifically ordered the old documents discarded. Pike had never inspected them. The admission seemed to (befuddle) him. He began to (gabble) about deadlines until Nora asked him to repeat the instruction, every (syllable). His wrongdoing might be less dramatic than a conspiracy, but its consequences were no less (lamentable). He had allowed ignorance to become a (stranglehold).

Kit was nearly (apoplectic). “I’d (swinge) the lot of them,” he said, borrowing a threat from the emperor’s script. Nora regarded him (askance). “You can argue about penalties later.” She understood his (outrage), but it was already acquiring a (manic) energy that made thought difficult. Destroyed papers, misunderstood instructions, and an embarrassed mayor were serious enough. They did not need imagined (carnage) to make them matter.

The discovery did not make Nora’s legal position (unassailable). A copy might be incomplete; another agreement might (precede) it. Nor could they infer intent from negligence alone. Kit, however, wanted to (pounce). “You let them (collude) behind our backs!” he said. Pike’s response became a (diatribe), rich in (bile) and poor in explanation. Nora asked both men to (disengage). Turning uncertainty into a public (spectacle) would (impede) the investigation. She would find someone qualified to read the deed. Until then, they could (bide) their time without attempting to (strangle) one another.

Unfortunately, a reporter had arrived. Her professional (antennae) were visibly alert. “Anything you’d like to (confide)?” she asked. Pike attempted to (dissuade) her from taking photographs. Kit was ready to (blab) about forty years of administrative failure. Nora handed over only the relevant page. “Please don’t (garble) this into a story about a stolen inheritance. My (parentage) is beside the point.” The hall belonged to a trust, if the document remained valid. Her grandmother’s family had no special claim. The reporter seemed disappointed, then interested. A village losing its own building through an (unchecked) assumption was, on reflection, quite a story.

They found the solicitor beside the cake stall, preparing to (amble) home. He was a (respectable) man whose vest buttons appeared ready to (bulge) outwards after a third helping of (trifle). Kit tried to (wheedle) free advice; Nora offered payment. The solicitor examined the seal, then the signatures. His face became (inscrutable). “A room,” he said. “And no speeches.” Pike began a (remonstrance). “Especially yours.” This was enough to (astound) Kit. They returned to the hall, where the solicitor could read without interruption. Outside, the first heavy drops began to fall.

Rain changed the fair’s mood in a (trice). Clouds that had seemed content to (scud) now delivered a (deluge). Families began to (converge) on the hall. Water threatened to (bedraggle) the dancers and ruin their costumes, so the organisers hurried them inside. Kit opened the main doors, then stopped people entering the damaged wing. A temporary (barricade) made from tables created a safe route. “Don’t (stampede),” he shouted. “There’s space.” Children who had been inclined to (straggle) suddenly found speed. A pony began to (prance); its rider slid from her (sidesaddle) seat into a helper’s arms. Nobody was hurt.

The storm’s violence made (drastic) changes to the programme unavoidable. “We must (hie) ourselves indoors!” the emperor shouted, helping a singer (scramble) off the platform. A violin case nearly opened, but Milo caught it. The youngest performers were too (excitable) to follow instructions until Nora asked them to (encircle) their teacher. They could carry on inside once the adults moved the equipment. The promise provided enough (reassurance) to keep them together.

The building filled with the (babble) of wet families. A (gaggle) of singers tried to (huddle) beside the stove while volunteers used towels to (swathe) valuable costumes. A duck escaped its handler and began to (waddle) towards the kitchen. Someone tried to (cadge) tea. Someone else wanted to (scrounge) a chair. The conductor attempted to (recommence) the concert, only for a microphone to (muffle) every second note. Nora watched a small boy with a (sniffle) begin to (toddle) towards the stage. His mother caught him. For all its faults, the supposedly useless building had become indispensable in fifteen minutes.

Then water appeared beneath the store-room door. At first it was a (trickle). Soon it began to (gurgle) around the threshold. Kit knew the blocked drain outside was responsible. If the water continued to rise, it would (choke) the old heating system. He asked Milo to fetch tools. Pike objected: volunteers must not attempt repairs. “Then help me find someone who can (plumb),” Kit snapped. He pulled a hose from the wall and (uncoiled) it across the floor. Nora used an empty (tankard) to scoop water away from a socket. The solicitor moved the documents onto the (mantelpiece), well clear of the spreading pool.

The yard had become a brown lake. Milo had to (trudge) through it, then (dodge) a floating (bale) of straw. Kit showed him where to (poke) the rod into the drain. At the third attempt, something shifted. A deep (gouge) in the paving channel revealed where a delivery vehicle had crushed its cover. Beyond it, roots formed a dense (tangle). Water pressed through with enough force to (entangle) the loose hose around Milo’s legs. He began to (wobble). Nora grabbed his (waistband) before he could (skid) backwards and (impale) himself on a broken fence post. For a moment all three could do nothing but (grapple) with the hose.

Pike appeared carrying a rope. He did not announce himself. He looped it around Milo and pulled with Nora until the boy was safe. The drain finally opened with a sound like an enormous animal clearing its throat. Water began to (recede). Milo stood shaking, physically (unscathed) but unable to (stifle) his tears. His uncle put a hand on his shoulder. Whatever else could be said of Pike, the gesture was not (melodramatic). Nora noticed his hand (tremble). “Good work, (laddie),” Kit said, abandoning hostility long enough to sound almost kind.

Inside, a cook produced a (bandage) for a scrape on Nora’s (knuckle). Another warned that a cooking pot might (scald) the children and moved it behind a screen. Damp clothes hung from every hook. A volunteer had to (ruffle) a dog’s fur dry before its owner would stop fussing. Nearby, a schoolgirl turned a broken umbrella into a dancing bird, with ribbon wings. Nora watched its bright feathers (waggle), then allowed herself a (giggle). The shock was beginning to (subside). Rain tapped against a circular (porthole) in the kitchen door. For the first time that day, she felt (solace) without needing to look backwards.

The solicitor emerged before anyone could (dawdle) over another argument. The trust was still active. Selling the hall required procedures that had not been followed. Neglect did not (entitle) the council to dispose of it as though it were an unwanted shed. He could not promise an (impregnable) case without further checks, but postponement was plainly (advisable). Pike would have to (concede) that much. Nora felt (elated), yet the solicitor’s next sentence stopped her. The building still needed a (sizable) sum. Discovering a right did not make the cost disappear. That truth was (inescapable), whatever the sentimental value of old letters.

Pike looked towards the crowded room. “We couldn’t maintain it,” he said. “Every repair cost (treble) what we’d planned.” For once he sounded (devoid) of performance. Nora believed him. The budget problem was real; so was his decision not to ask for help. His (erstwhile) certainty had protected him from admitting failure. Kit began to (grumble), then stopped. There was a difference between wanting a man’s defeat and wanting a building saved. “It doesn’t have to be (unmanageable),” Nora said. “But we need actual figures.” The mayor nodded. His expression was awkwardly (apologetic). It was not forgiveness, but it might be a beginning.

The reporter suggested an announcement. Nora refused a victory speech. Such a speech would only (rile) Pike’s supporters and turn caution into (cowardice) in the eyes of her own. She would neither (commend) neglect nor pretend (malice) had been proved. Instead, she asked everyone to listen. A child gave the bell a (jangle), and the room quietened. “The sale is paused,” she said. “That does not mean the roof repairs are free.” A (chuckle) travelled through the audience. “We need skills, money, and people willing to do ordinary jobs.” A carpenter put up his hand. Then a bookkeeper. Then the woman who cleaned the school.

Enthusiasm began to (pervade) the hall. A teacher who had (refereed) the morning’s games offered to organise next year’s tournament. A retired decorator could (gild) the damaged lettering; a gardener would tackle the (mould) only after a professional assessed its cause. Two teenagers volunteered to (daub) test colours on scrap wood. The kitchen team promised a (hygienic) reopening. A musician proposed lessons; a seamstress would teach children to work on an (inkle) weaving frame. Kit warned against trying to (cobble) everything together in a weekend. Good intentions deserved proper planning.

To buy time, the fair continued indoors. The theatre company offered an improvised show about a (maniac) emperor whose accountants had turned (demonic). The plot was (lurid), the acting (erratic), and the jokes largely concerned tax. An (overage) prince attempted to (unsheathe) a wooden sword; a (banshee) replied with a (cackle). The emperor’s feathered (hackle) caught in a curtain. “This is a (veritable) disaster!” he declared, while the audience watched (spellbound). A small child pointed out that this was precisely the story. The resulting laughter seemed to (resound) through rooms that had been silent for months.

Kit worried that one old script used the offensive word “(paleface)”. Nora removed that scene; preserving a place did not require preserving every lazy insult ever spoken in it. Elsewhere, a magician tried to (juggle) a (satsuma), a (bauble), and a knitted (bobble). Children would (goggle) when he let one (dangle) from his ear. He managed to (bungle) the finale, but a helpful (tyke) supplied the missing fruit. Another performer proposed to (spreadeagle) himself between chairs until the solicitor offered a single raised eyebrow. Sometimes (vigilance) worked better than a page of rules.

The cooks assembled a supper from whatever remained: (rhubarb) pudding, bread with (treacle), and cheese with (pickle). “A culinary (miscarriage),” declared the emperor, helping himself twice. One woman rescued a (breakable) dish from the edge of a table. Another found a glass (shard) and swept it away before anyone could (tread) on it. A boy tried to (dribble) a football under the chairs until Kit sent him (upfield), towards an empty corridor. Outside, a delivery (sledge) served as a temporary bridge over the worst (pothole). Repairs were already beginning, in the modest form of people noticing what needed doing.

At a quiet table, Nora found Milo trying to (scribble) an apology. He would (crumple) each sheet almost immediately. “You don’t need to (plead),” she told him. He said he felt like a (dunce). She disagreed. He had obeyed an adult and then told the truth when doing so became difficult. That was a (creditable) recovery. His actions at the drain had been (admirable), too. He began to (twiddle) his pen, trying not to smile. A (dimple) appeared. Nora resisted the urge to (mollycoddle) him. “Next time, ask what’s in the boxes.” He nodded. That, at least, was a lesson he could use.

Pike joined them with three cups of tea. Kit followed, plainly expecting a (tussle). Instead, the mayor admitted he had found it easier to sell a problem than to explain it. He was not (invincible), he said, and never had been. Kit considered an insulting reply, then settled for silence. “A (feeble) excuse,” Pike added. “But the real one.” Nora asked him to (uphold) the postponement in writing. He agreed. They would (prearrange) a survey, publish the accounts, and let qualified people identify the next (hurdle). If costs proved impossible, the village would at least face them with its eyes open.

Not everyone welcomed the compromise. One woman threatened to (flounce) out because she wanted Pike removed immediately. Another began to (seethe) over the cost. The reporter received a (jab) of criticism for failing to expose a grand plot. Nora knew no agreement could avoid every (annoyance), every (squabble), or every attempt to (wangle) an advantage. Someone would always (peddle) a (tarradiddle). But she refused to let the desire for a perfect ending (upend) a useful one. The choice was between working together and watching the walls (crumble). Bellweather had done quite enough of the latter.

By evening, donations and volunteer names began to (abound). A (raffle) brought an unexpected (upsurge) in cash. Visitors paid two pounds (apiece) to guess the weight of an enormous marrow, then stayed to (mingle). Children helped (spangle) the backdrop with paper stars. Old friends began to (reminisce); newcomers could (intermingle) without needing a family connection. The hall’s value was becoming (recognisable) in the simplest possible way: people were using it. Nora watched a grandmother try to (tickle) a laughing baby while a teenager helped an older neighbour (hobble) to a chair. No brochure could have explained the argument better.

The children’s painting stall reopened with water beginning to (speckle) the paper from someone’s wet hair. A toddler wanted to (dabble) both hands in blue paint; her sister preferred to (doodle) an elaborate crown. A mother tried to smooth a (wrinkle) from a costume only for its owner to (wriggle) away. Paper hats would (crinkle) whenever their wearers moved. One little dancer insisted that she needed room to (wiggle), and the bookkeeper readily shifted his chair.

Kit found Nora by the stage. “Didn’t think you’d stay,” he said. She admitted she had intended to (forsake) the village as efficiently as possible. He showed no (reverence) for her change of heart. “Don’t make a religion of the place. Half of us are impossible.” She laughed. She had no desire to (seclude) herself here, nor to (delude) herself about what restoring it would demand. Still, she could come back for meetings. The prospect no longer made her (cringe).

Behind them, someone (uncorked) the last bottle of lemonade. Bells from the costumes gave a faint (tinkle), and the dog returned for a hopeful (snuffle) beneath the food table. Kit began to (ramble) about the building’s former (prominence) until Nora gently interrupted. They would have to (contend) with the present first. He nodded, then tried to (sidle) away before she could give him another job. She handed him a broom. She picked up her grandmother’s brooch. It was tarnished and missing a stone, but it was enough.

After the storm, sunlight began to (dapple) the courtyard. A cart horse lifted a (hind) leg while its owner adjusted the harness. An actor called it his noble (steed), climbed aboard with a grand (stride), and immediately complained about his (backside). A loose (protuberance) on the seat had caught him; Kit inspected its (underside) and removed a nail. Children began to (ogle) the horse until its owner asked them to stand back. From the garden stall came a warning that (belladonna), (monkshood), and (wormwood) were display plants, not ingredients. Their labels had survived the rain better than most of the publicity.

The last visitors helped to (trundle) tables into storage. Somebody found the missing microscope (eyepiece) from the school display; somebody else retrieved a toy (manacle) from the stage. Two children tried to (scavenge) leftover sweets, while a dog continued to (forage) beneath the benches. Kit caught a boy about to (unhinge) a cupboard door and redirected his energy. “You don’t have to (maraud) through the place to help.” A volunteer had nearly managed to (singe) a cloth against a heater, so Nora moved it. Affection alone did not make a building safe. Attention did.

At the entrance, Pike hesitated. “Your grandmother would have enjoyed this,” he said. Nora looked at his tired (visage). Perhaps she would. Or perhaps she would have delivered a twenty-minute account of everything they had overlooked. The thought brought a (twinge), but not the familiar urge to escape it.

Milo arrived with a box of salvaged photographs. “Found these in the (wreckage),” he (piped), then blushed at the exaggeration. Pike helped him stack them flat so the damp would not (rumple) the prints. “We’ll need to (redouble) our efforts tomorrow,” the mayor said. For once, Nora heard no election slogan in it. The afternoon’s (kerfuffle) had left a small (ripple) of change in the way they spoke to one another. They could go (onward) from there.

She could allow (reminiscence) without making the past a (shroud). Behind her, the orchestra tried one final piece. The sound was irregular, yet there was a (brilliance) in hearing it here at all. She felt briefly (awed), then reached for a broom.

The building would not survive on one afternoon’s (defiance). Its problems were (interlocked), and money remained scarce. A fresh (resurgence) of goodwill might fade; public affection was (fickle). Nora knew enthusiasm could (ebb) as quickly as it arrived. But the day had exposed what ought to (underlie) any decision about the hall: knowledge of what people stood to lose. Tomorrow there would be estimates, objections, and more (discord). Tonight, a repaired lamp gave a small (twinkle) above the stairs. Saving the place might (disgruntle) almost everyone at some point. It would also give them somewhere to meet.
translation:
拒绝被出售的村庄

还没到中午，镇长就已威胁要关闭(游乐场)，一只(捕鸟蛛)从学校的动物展棚里逃了出来，而诺拉·贝尔则发现，有人打算把她祖母的信件(埋葬)在一家超市的停车场下面。只有前两件事引起了公众注意。贝尔韦瑟的居民在陷入(歇斯底里)这件事上有着惊人的(天赋)，但面对书面文件时，反应通常十分(迟钝)。诺拉这次回来是为了卖掉祖母的房子，原以为会度过一个安静的周末。没想到，她竟站在一株(绣球花)旁，手里拿着一封带有(压纹)的信，琢磨究竟该在镇长演讲前还是演讲后把他(拦住问个究竟)。

信上的(收件人)是埃莉诺·马什，(娘家姓)贝尔。信中，一位律师说市场礼堂是为村民“(永久)”持有的财产。这与镇长提议周一就将它(拆除)的计划很难相容。诺拉的祖母在这里度过了四十年，教孩子们(揉)面包面团，也教大人们如何为暖气费(讨价还价)。她认为，给委员会(当牛做马)是一种荣誉，前提是偶尔可以(得罪)一下主席。诺拉继承了她的(花梨木)针线盒、一只银(手镯)，以及一封叮嘱她别让“那个(精明的)小个子男人”卖掉礼堂的信。她原以为，这不过是一场陈年(宿怨)最后的余音。

派克镇长已经站在台上。他本来是个(不起眼的)男人，留着精心修剪的(山羊胡)，可只要配上一支麦克风，就变得(令人招架不住)。他的开场(引言)谈的是效率；接下来的十分钟则(催眠)得足以让一匹喝过咖啡的马也(脑子发蒙)。他解释说，这座礼堂是个(旧时代的遗物)，管道设施(不合标准)，修复几乎是(不可能完成的)。拆除将为繁荣提供一块(跳板)。附近一张(杂乱的)桌子旁，管理员带着(讥讽的)神情看着他。“他可以一直(高谈阔论)到圣诞节，”他对诺拉说，“可还是解释不了，为什么他要卖一栋根本不属于他的房子。”

管理员叫基特。他的(胡茬)、打着补丁的(长上衣)，以及那副常年(龇牙咧嘴的表情)，使他看上去像个失业的巫师。他(脾气暴躁)，常常(烦躁易怒)，也算不上多么(讨人喜欢)，不过他曾经通宵为幼儿园免费修好暖气。人们把他当成一个(怪人)，不太拿他当回事。派克更喜欢叫他“(疯子)”。基特则称派克为(大笨蛋)，随后又向一名碰巧听见的真正的小学生道了歉。“我和你祖母是(亲自打过交道)的，”他说，“她并不总是对的。但她能从一个男人折发票的方式，(推断出)他在做什么不诚实的勾当。”他仔细看了看信。头一次，他的神情(阴沉下来)。

通常，没有什么能让基特(心神不宁)。水管爆了，他随意挥挥手；有人投诉，他就(不慌不忙地)请对方自己去修。但这封信可能(推翻)整个重建计划。“你最好(重视)这件事，”他说。诺拉问他是否认识律师。“好几个。大多数已经不肯再(帮我忙)了。”他翻了翻口袋，掏出一(沓)旧收据。其中夹着一个电话号码。这是一个计划最初的(雏形)。

他们周围，贝尔韦瑟的居民正享受着(数不清的)小小乐趣。孩子们可以在一座(可折叠的)城堡旁(嬉戏)，大人们则排队买一根(小香肠)、一勺(蛋奶酱)，或者一罐(柑橘果酱)。园艺协会展出了一盆(秋海棠)、一盆(蔓长春花)，还有几株长势格外旺盛的(欧当归)。一丛(灌木)后面，青少年乐团正在尝试演奏一首(小夜曲)，他们对(节奏)的把握显然比音准更有信心。一位面包师用(长柄勺)倒面糊，她的丈夫则试图一边(切碎)洋葱，一边(赶走)一条狗。热糖的香气是一剂令人愉快的(强心剂)。诺拉本来打算买份午餐，(午睡)一会儿，然后离开。现在，她连一块饼干都几乎(啃不下)。

台上，派克还在继续许诺。基特认为那都是代价高昂的(空话)。他旁边的一位店主更愿意称之为“(胡说八道)”。两个人都不肯(鼓掌)，尽管镇长的支持者表现出了显而易见的(欢喜)。一个男孩开始(模仿)派克的手势，直到母亲制止了他。“他又不是个(歇斯底里的人)，”她说，“你也不是。”男孩摆出一副尊严受损的表情。平时，这一幕会逗乐诺拉。可今天，她只能对着那只信封(忧心忡忡)。

基特带她从侧门走进礼堂。一丛(荆棘)霸占了排水沟，(金银花)紧贴着窗玻璃。里面的空气有股(陈腐的)味道，还夹着(一丝)(刺鼻的)气息。一汪(积水)映出一个石膏(小天使)，不巧的是，它和镇长颇为(相像)。油漆开始(剥落)，一面墙被孔洞(蛀得千疮百孔)。一个柜子里放着(变质的)抛光剂、一(团)凝固的胶，以及一粒已经石化的面包(碎屑)。“这里确实疏于照料，”诺拉说。“当然，”基特答道，“但当个(邋遢鬼)，不等于你就拥有这个地方。”一块护墙板后面传来轻轻的(搏动声)，仿佛这栋楼有一颗紧张的心。

基特停下了脚步。声音也停了。楼上本该(无人居住)。诺拉觉得衣领下面泛起一阵(刺痒)。基特拿起一把(铁锹)，想了想，又放下了。“不要(流血)，”他说，“对保险不好。”他们开始(上楼)。在楼梯平台上，诺拉不得不把袖子从一根仍(突出)栏杆的钉子上(解脱出来)。一扇门敞开着。门后，一个(独自一人)的男孩戴着(头套)，正试图把一只旧箱子(吃力地搬到)一辆带轮子的(平板小车)上。他看起来像是(被逼到了死角)。随后他脚下一滑，箱子(砰的一声)落了地。

男孩是派克的侄子迈洛，一个(胆小的)十六岁少年，鼻子上有颗(雀斑)，下巴上有一颗格外醒目的(青春痘)。他摘下面罩，露出一张(苍白)、满是(痛苦不安)的脸。“灰尘，”他指着那块布解释道，“我找不到别的东西。”他原以为只是来搬垃圾，没想到会遇见目击者。基特开始(刺激)他，诺拉却出面制止了。她不愿让一个受惊的孩子在还没有人听过他的解释之前，就被(架着赶出)房间。她让迈洛坐下。一场(无端的)攻击只会(激怒)他的叔叔，也会让唯一可能(透露)实情的人(不敢再开口)。

“他们让我(提前)清理干净，”迈洛说，“周一之前。买方那边的那个(家伙)说，不会有人介意。”诺拉叫他不要(撒谎)。他盯着自己的鞋。“我没有。”基特找到一把(折叠小刀)，把箱子上一块松动的黄铜片(拧了下来)。箱盖纹丝不(动)，于是诺拉小心地在角上(推了一下)。里面传来金属的(咔嚓声)。内部的搭扣卡住了，配件里的一小块(楔形固定片)滑了位。两人一起设法把它(弄了出来)。“别把文件(弄坏了)，”基特提醒道，“它们比箱子值钱。”迈洛试着(呼出一口气)，尽量不让自己听上去像是吓坏了。

里面(乱七八糟地堆着)账目、照片和戏服。一个(紫褐色的)文件夹用(编织带)绑着。在一条虫蛀的(床罩)下面，诺拉发现一本账簿，记着用(金属货币)支付的款项、一场为(孤儿院)募款的活动所交的租金，以及救济包裹按重量收取的(邮费)。一张发票涉及一张捐赠的(床架)、配套的(床头板)，以及用(驳船)运输的费用。一张照片里，祖母(跨在)一辆坏自行车上，笑得很开心。诺拉本来已经做好准备，要(割舍)自己对贝尔韦瑟的感情。可看到这一幕，她却(心里一痛)。她坐在箱子上，忽然无法再演出自己练习了一整周的那种(公事公办的)冷淡。

这些戏服属于一出讲述骗子皇帝的业余戏剧。其中有一件(古罗马长袍)、一副破旧的(单片眼镜)、一条橡胶(触手)，以及一个空(剑鞘)。两个信封里装着假胡子：一个写着“(小胡子，美式拼法)”，另一个写着“(小胡子，英式拼法)”。就连道具委员会也能为这类细节(争论不休)。一张草图画着一个机械怪物，一半是(鸡蛇怪)，一半是(水马妖)，原本是用来(喷出)碎纸的。它的嘴雕刻得极其仔细，甚至有人在上腭的一条(皱襞)旁作了标注。“这是你祖母做的，”基特说，“她退休前是牙科护士。”一枚(圣甲虫)胸针从戏服堆里掉了出来。诺拉立刻认出了它。她扮演(小精灵)时，祖母曾允许她戴上这枚胸针。

回忆开始(涌上心头，将她淹没)。她想起那道(诡异的)蓝光、观众的(喧闹)，以及自己为避免(绊倒)而作出的(慌乱的)努力。祖母曾轻声说：“不管(发生什么)，都要继续。”一个木制的(丘比特)从布景上掉了下来，一枚舞台(手榴弹)则成了(哑弹)。皇帝即兴来了一个(滑稽的)鞠躬，把事故变成了喜剧。如今，账簿里夹着一张节目单，上面有一行(清晰可辨的)说明：全部收入都将用于保护礼堂，使其免遭私人出售。这个承诺既不(空洞)，也不含糊。诺拉第一次感到怒意(隐隐涌起)。“真正的契约在哪里？”

这个问题打断了基特自己的(遐想)。他记得有一场在夏至这一(至日)举行的会议，有人争论过出售计划，之后文件便被锁了起来。随之而来的是多年的(纷争)，再后来，当事人都老了。仅仅因为没有人记得归档方式，一个承诺竟然就能从整个村庄的记忆中(消失)，这实在荒唐。“除非，”基特说，“它(或许)还在这里。”他满怀希望又一本正经的措辞，差点让诺拉笑出来。她开始检查每一个口袋和袖子，盼着那份失踪的文件(重新出现)。

迈洛开始(笨手笨脚地翻找)那些纸张。“还有一个箱子。”他的声音低成了(咕哝)。那个箱子早上已经被搬进了垃圾箱。基特骂了一句颇有分量的(脏话)。诺拉一时(惊慌得)动弹不得。随后，祖母的嘱托显得几乎像是(预言)。他们必须沿着男孩走过的路线(原路返回)，到垃圾箱里(翻找)，并祈祷雨水还没有把里面的东西泡成纸浆。基特想要(指控)有人蓄意销毁证据。诺拉坚持先查清事实。只有(一丝)怀疑是不(够的)，无论想象中的(报应)会多么令人痛快。

外面，镇长的演讲已经让位于宠物巡游。一只流着大量(口水)的(猎狼犬)正在打量一只(猎野猪犬)，旁边一位女士试图(安抚)一个开始(长牙)的婴儿。动物展棚里，一只(鬣蜥)趴在一个(蠵龟)模型旁。逃走的蜘蛛已在水族箱后的一箱(海藻)里找到了。它的主人抱怨，人们总给无害的爱好贴上(污名)。一只蓝色的(虎皮鹦鹉)被放回(鸟笼)后，发出了尖锐的现场评论。诺拉试着在人群中(穿行)。基特跟在后面，还得(挡开)一名执意想让他担任鸟类(羽毛)比赛评委的组织者。

垃圾箱在(教堂墓地)外面，一道老旧的(越栏梯)通向卸货场。诺拉的鞋被一颗(小石子)绊住，翻过去时险些(失去平衡)。迈洛递来一根(柔韧的)树枝让她扶着。地上，一群(潮虫)在一个基特认为属于(睡鼠)的窝旁四散而逃。一只(田鼠)在被人(踩到)之前消失了。他们头顶的石头(凸台)上，幼鸟已经快要(羽翼丰满)。一切似乎都执意照常过自己的日子。诺拉羡慕这种笃定。她自己的计划，不到一个小时就已被扔在了(半路上)。

有人把厨余垃圾倒在了箱子上。气味(腐臭难闻)。一只被扔掉的(朝鲜蓟)、一条橙子(皮)，以及一整份毁掉的(牛奶冻)，都压在文件上。基特试着用棍子把它们(捞出来)。迈洛不得不在两个垃圾袋之间(扭动身体)，才能够到底部，嘴里嘟囔着自己可能会(吐)。“别吐，”基特说，“我们这里的材料已经够多了。”诺拉撑着袋口，一只纠缠不休的(小飞虫)让她不断(抖动)肩膀。终于，一包带着水渍的东西露了出来。隔着一块(污迹)，仍能(辨认出)那枚(泄露线索的)蓝色印章。她几乎(欣喜若狂)，直到一个熟悉的声音说道：“把那个放下。”

迈洛吓得猛然向远离垃圾箱的方向(一冲)。他的手肘撞到了箱沿，一张纸飞了出去。诺拉在排水沟的(边缘)及时接住了它。派克来得几乎过于巧合，但这只是一次(偶然)，不能证明他们受到了监视。篱笆外，一名志愿者正在抱怨一条狗留下的(粪便)，另一名则忙着(分发)防雨罩。他们那些平常的烦恼，与诺拉突如其来的困境形成的反差，足以让她(目瞪口呆)。

派克站在门口，看上去(气得脸色铁青)。他那种(漫不经心的)态度消失了，取而代之的是一个发现下午的局面已失去控制的人身上，那种(清晰可感的)愤怒。“这简直(卑鄙)，”他说。基特刚要回答，诺拉便抬起手，免得争吵演变成(扭打)。她不会让一场关于礼貌的争执(压过)证据。派克指责他们搞(破坏)，把这次寻找说成一场(胡闹横行)，还说他们无权(插手)。最后这个词说错了。过去二十年里，诺拉不断被人告诫不要多管闲事。此刻她发现，自己已经不在乎了。

“是你让迈洛把这些东西搬走的吗？”她问。派克试图用一番关于保险的解释(回避)问题。基特发出一声(讥诮的)笑。迈洛盯着草地。“你可以等会儿再(责备)我，”诺拉说，“现在先回答他。”派克的沉默似乎比愤怒更让男孩(心神大乱)。终于，迈洛开口了。镇长要求清空房间，但具体下令扔掉旧文件的，是买方代表。派克从未查看过那些文件。这个事实似乎把他(弄糊涂了)。他开始(急促而含混地说着)截止日期，直到诺拉要求他把指示逐字逐句、每一个(音节)都重复清楚。他的过错也许不如阴谋那样戏剧化，但后果同样(可悲)。他任由无知变成了一种(牢牢的控制)。

基特几乎(暴跳如雷)。“我非得把他们全都(狠狠惩治)一顿，”他说，借用了皇帝剧本里的一句威胁。诺拉(不以为然地斜看)了他一眼。“处罚的事可以以后再争。”她理解他的(义愤)，但那股情绪已经带上了令人难以思考的(狂躁)劲头。被毁的文件、被误解的指示，以及一个难堪的镇长，本身就已经足够严重。没必要再想象一场(大屠杀)，才能显得它们重要。

这个发现并没有让诺拉在法律上变得(无懈可击)。副本可能不完整，也可能另有一份协议(早于)它存在。他们也不能仅凭疏忽就推断动机。然而基特已经想要(扑上去发难)。“你让他们背着我们(串通)！”他说。派克的回应变成了一场(长篇痛骂)，充满(怨毒)，却没多少解释。诺拉请两个人先(停止纠缠)。把尚未确定的事情变成一场公开的(闹剧)，只会(妨碍)调查。她会找个有资格的人来解读契约。在那之前，他们完全可以(耐心等待)，不必试图把对方(掐死)。

不巧的是，一名记者已经到了。她那职业性的(触角)显然十分敏锐。“有什么愿意(私下告诉)我的吗？”她问。派克试图(劝阻)她拍照。基特则已经准备好，把四十年来的管理失误统统(抖露出来)。诺拉只交给她相关的那一页。“请不要把这件事(歪曲)成一篇遗产被偷的故事。我的(家世)与此无关。”如果这份文件依然有效，礼堂就属于一个信托。她祖母的家人没有任何特殊权利。记者似乎有些失望，随后又来了兴趣。一个村庄竟因一项(未经核查的)假定而失去自己的建筑，仔细想想，这还真是个故事。
